summary: Mission Control lets anyone design, launch and operate a real space mission. Players balance mass, power, money, data and fuel, pass a NASA-style Go/No-Go poll, survive solar storms and get a scored engineering debrief. Pixel, a robot co-pilot, makes it easy for beginners, while real orbital mechanics and link budgets run underneath.
details:
The problem. Space engineering is exciting, but its core lesson is hard to feel from a textbook: every decision is a trade-off. Bigger instruments need more power, more power needs bigger solar panels, panels add mass, mass needs a bigger rocket, and the rocket costs money you don't have.

What we built. Mission Control is a complete, playable mission design game in a single web page. Players choose one of five missions (Earth, Moon, Mars, asteroids, deep space), build a spacecraft from 23 components, pick an orbit and a rocket, then launch. Seven live gauges show whether the design works, and the mission simulation runs on the player's actual numbers. A weak radio really loses data, a thin power margin really causes brownouts, and too little fuel really leaves the spacecraft in the wrong orbit.

Easy and fun. Pixel, a robot co-pilot, gives step-by-step quests. One-click "Fix it" buttons solve problems and explain what changed. Players earn stars, XP, ranks, badges and Space Credits to spend on research upgrades and paint jobs. Their agency's funding grows as they fly better missions, so skill unlocks bigger budgets.

Real engineering. Under the friendly surface, every number comes from a published method:

  • vis-viva orbital mechanics and Hohmann transfers
  • the rocket equation
  • SMAD solar power sizing with eclipse geometry
  • full decibel link budgets to NASA's Deep Space Network
  • TRL-based mass growth
  • a 5×5 risk matrix

A "∑ math" button on every gauge shows the equations with the player's own numbers. The results match real missions: a 1,847 m/s burn to reach geostationary orbit, and a 259-day cruise to Mars.

What makes it different. It works for a 16-year-old on their first try, and it holds up when an engineer checks the math. It is transparent about what is simplified, with a Methods page that lists every equation and source.

How it works (tech)

Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS in one self-contained file, with Three.js for 3D, Canvas for orbit diagrams, ground tracks and charts, and the Web Audio API for sound. Progress is saved with localStorage. There is no install and no build step: open index.html and play.

Challenges we ran into

  • Making real physics produce good gameplay. We tuned the reference designs so each mission is winnable, while weaker designs fail for real engineering reasons.
  • Explaining decibel link budgets and power sizing to beginners without hiding them. The answer was two layers: plain-language gauges on top and ∑ math panels underneath.

What's next

  • Online multiplayer across devices with Supabase Realtime.
  • A shared global leaderboard.
  • Landers and rovers as new mission types.
